title: Nithya Raman: The City of Angels’ New DSA Mayor
author: Youth Outsider Editorial Team
dek: A democratic socialist who entered the race at the last minute just unseated Mayor Karen Bass. Now she has to govern a city whose council backed her opponent.
cover_alt: Collage of Nithya Raman, Karen Bass, Los Angeles City Hall and the Palisades fire

body:
Los Angeles has a new mayor, and she is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. City Councilmember Nithya Raman led Mayor Karen Bass [52.7% to 47.3%](https://mynewsla.com/government/2026/11/05/raman-wins-la-mayors-race-bass-concedes-promises-smooth-transition-7/) when Bass conceded on Thursday, with Raman's lead growing to more than 47,000 votes. She is the first challenger to unseat a sitting Los Angeles mayor since 2005, and the Asian Democrats of Los Angeles County called her the [first Asian American](https://aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/6/city-of-immigrants-who-is-nithya-raman-the-los-angeles-mayor-elect) elected to lead the city.

*"Los Angeles, I'm deeply honored to be your next mayor,"* Raman said in a video statement. Bass wrote that *"the people of Los Angeles have spoken"* and promised a smooth transition. Raman takes office on Dec. 14.

Raman, 45, was born in Kerala, India, and moved to the United States with her family when she was 6. She grew up in Louisiana, became a citizen at 22, and studied at Harvard before earning a master's in urban planning from MIT. She went back to India to run a research group that worked on sanitation and city services in Chennai.

She moved to Los Angeles in 2013, worked for the city's administrative officer, and in 2017 co-founded the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition, a group of neighbors in Silver Lake and nearby areas helping unhoused people. She later ran Time's Up Entertainment, the group that funds legal help for victims of sexual harassment in Hollywood.

In 2020, backed by the local DSA chapter, she beat City Councilmember David Ryu, [52.9% to 47.1%](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nithya_Raman). It was the first time in 17 years a challenger had unseated a sitting councilmember. She won reelection in 2024 without a runoff and became one of the council's leading voices on housing and homelessness.

Raman and Bass were allies. Raman had endorsed Bass for reelection, and less than two weeks later, in February, she [entered the race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Los_Angeles_mayoral_election) hours before the filing deadline. Bass's allies called it a betrayal.

The June primary was a three-way race. Bass finished first with 34.3%, Raman second with 29%, and Spencer Pratt, a Republican reality TV star who lost his home in the Palisades fire, third with 25.5%. That set up a runoff between two Democrats.

Bass had almost the entire establishment behind her: Kamala Harris, Gov. Gavin Newsom, Nancy Pelosi, both of California's senators, most of the city's major unions and the police union. Raman had the Los Angeles chapter of DSA, which endorsed her in September, along with hotel workers in UNITE HERE Local 11, the Writers Guild of America West, the Working Families Party and City Controller Kenneth Mejia.

She won anyway. Voters were angry about the city's response to the January 2025 Palisades fire and a 2026 warehouse fire in Boyle Heights, and Raman built her campaign around the basics. Occidental College political scientist Caroline Heldman said Raman [*"positioned herself as the pothole politician, very similar to Zohran Mamdani,"*](https://www.click2houston.com/news/politics/2026/11/07/nithya-raman-to-take-charge-in-la-amid-homeless-crisis-and-political-division/) the democratic socialist who won New York's mayoral race last year. She talked about fixing streets, lights and sidewalks more than about sweeping socialist programs, and she rode a national wave that saw Democrats sweep the midterms.

The race between former friends turned bitter. At their October debate, Raman called Bass's tenure [*"four years of decline, of mismanagement, of excuses,"*](https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/10/la-mayoral-debate-friends-feud/) and said the mayor had been "MIA" during and after the Palisades fire. Bass accused Raman of lying about her record and warned that *"now is not the time to turn the city over to Nithya Raman."*

The two clashed over housing. Bass pointed to 10,000 new affordable units built on her watch. Raman pointed out that overall apartment construction was falling and accused Bass of paying "lip service" to cutting the red tape that blocks new buildings.

They fought over policing. Raman said LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell had lost the trust of immigrant communities during federal immigration raids and that she would seek his removal. She criticized Bass's billion-dollar police pay deal and a $2.6 billion convention center expansion. Bass warned that Raman would throw the LAPD into "disarray," and the police union spent about $3 million to defeat her.

And they fought at City Hall. In August, Council President Marqueece Harris-Dawson, Bass's closest ally on the council, split the housing and homelessness committee Raman had chaired since 2023, leaving her without either post. *"I might be getting punished for running against Mayor Bass,"* [Raman said](https://laist.com/news/nithya-raman-out-chair-la-city-councils-homelessness-committee-dawson-bass).

Raman has made homelessness her first priority. She says she will audit *"every dollar spent on homelessness"* on her first day in office. Her [plan](https://www.nbclosangeles.com/news/local/nithya-raman-plans-los-angeles/3967166/) would expand street medicine teams for unhoused people, cap stays in city-funded motels at 120 days before moving people into apartments with up to two years of rent help, and send an outreach worker within 48 hours whenever residents report an encampment. Her goal is to cut the number of people living in tents in half before the 2028 Olympics.

On housing, she has promised to triple the pace of construction. On policing, she wants unarmed crisis teams to answer some nonviolent 911 calls, says she will not cut LAPD staffing, and wants the department to pay for its own lawsuit settlements, which cost the city about $150 million last year. On immigration, she would bar the LAPD from working with ICE and ban ICE operations on city property. And on the basics, she has promised to repave streets, not just patch potholes, and to bring film and TV jobs back to Los Angeles.

None of Raman's 14 council colleagues endorsed her. Thirteen backed Bass, [LAist reported](https://laist.com/news/politics/mayor-elect-nithya-raman-council-colleagues-cooperation), including the two other DSA members on the council, Eunisses Hernandez and Ysabel Jurado. In Los Angeles, the council approves the budget and the mayor's appointments, so almost every promise Raman made will need their votes.

Some of her new colleagues have made their feelings clear. Councilmember Imelda Padilla, who represents part of the San Fernando Valley, once called serving on Raman's homelessness committee the *"most unproductive time I've had on the council."* After the election, she congratulated Raman online and said she looked forward to building bridges between the Valley and City Hall. Councilmember Monica Rodriguez said during the campaign that she didn't know what Raman stood for, and afterward said working together would require colleagues to set aside "personal feelings." Councilmember Traci Park, whose Westside district includes the Palisades, criticized Raman's record on public safety and fire response.

Others sounded warmer. Harris-Dawson said the city should *"come together and build a bright future."* Councilmember Katy Yaroslavsky, one of only two members who joined Raman in voting against the convention center deal, said *"dysfunction is a choice."*

Raman's supporters say she already has. She spent six years in City Hall, chaired its housing and homelessness committee for three years. Her platform looks less like a revolution than a to-do list: audits, repaved streets, faster housing permits. She has described herself as both a capitalist and a democratic socialist, and when asked about the comparison to Mamdani, she said, *"But I am different. I am myself."*

Her critics see three problems. The first is experience: she has never run anything close to a city government with tens of thousands of employees. The second is the council, which can block her budget and her appointments. The third is her own movement. Some DSA members say she has not gone far enough, especially on Israel, and the national organization narrowly voted down a move to withdraw its endorsement of her over her position on boycotts of Israel. Police accountability activists say they will pressure her from day one, while the police union predicted disaster if she won.

The problems waiting for her are real. The city's budget is strained, tens of thousands of people are homeless, the Palisades is still rebuilding, and the 2028 Olympics are less than two years away. *"I can't think of a mayor who had to take office with so many problems,"* said former Councilmember Mike Bonin. *"Everybody leaves unpopular."*

Whether Raman proves him wrong will be the best test yet of whether a democratic socialist can run one of America's biggest cities.
